title: Depression, Low Mood & Motivation
description: First unit: Sadness after disappointment. Work through real situations, competing explanations and practical choices.

lessons.title: What is really happening?
lessons.teach: Callum has felt sad and unmotivated since failing to get a job he hoped would change his situation. Jules calls to check in.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Listen closely to what each person says and what still remains uncertain.
nodes.explanation: Sadness following disappointment is understandable. Withdrawal can reduce immediate social demands but also reduce access to rewarding experiences, which may maintain low mood.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.
nodes.scenario: Callum has felt sad and unmotivated since failing to get a job he hoped would change his situation. Jules calls to check in.

options.feedback: The strength of a feeling matters, but it does not establish its cause.

options.feedback: This gathers information that could strengthen or weaken the explanation, rather than merely confirming an impression.

options.label: Ask the person affected whether the behaviour seems consistent with their overall impression of the speaker.
options.feedback: Impact and perception matter for responding; they are less decisive about the other person’s hidden motives.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A student feels low after a breakup and gradually stops attending activities that previously provided enjoyment, even as the initial acute distress changes.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

nodes.title: Apply the method elsewhere
nodes.prompt: Consider this different situation: A student feels low after a breakup and gradually stops attending activities that previously provided enjoyment, even as the initial acute distress changes. What is the strongest next step?
nodes.explanation: Transfer the reasoning method rather than an explanation from the first case. A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.
options.feedback: This asks what the behaviour might accomplish and how we could check.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

nodes.title: Fact or inference?
nodes.prompt: Sort the exact words spoken from explanations about what those words might mean.
nodes.explanation: The words are evidence. Both the preferred explanation and its rival are interpretations requiring further testing. A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.

Callum may need time to grieve a meaningful loss; a short period of retreat is not automatically a maladaptive cycle.

nodes.title: Build the psychological process
nodes.prompt: Arrange this possible sequence. One step concerns what the person might be thinking; treat it as a hypothesis.

He cancels plans for temporary relief
Fewer rewarding encounters may prolong withdrawal and low mood

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Sadness following disappointment is understandable. Withdrawal can reduce immediate social demands but also reduce access to rewarding experiences, which may maintain low mood.

A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.
